articles.title: Bringing Spanish Purchases into the United States
articles.excerpt: One of Spain's most iconic purchases is also one Americans can't legally bring home in their luggage — here's what's actually restricted and what isn't.
articles.content:
Most souvenirs from Spain sail through US customs without a second thought — but one of the country's most iconic purchases is a genuine exception, and it catches Americans off guard often enough that it deserves its own warning before you're standing in a jamonería with your wallet out.

The one you can't bring home: cured ham

Under US federal regulation (9 CFR 94.31), cured hams — including jamón ibérico and jamón serrano — from Spain, along with similar cured pork products from France, Germany and Italy, may not be brought into the United States by travelers in personal luggage. This isn't a vague guideline; it's a real, enforced restriction, and travelers really have had ham confiscated at the border over it. The only legal path for this product into the US is a commercial shipment from a USDA/FDA-approved Spanish processing establishment — not something an individual buying a leg of jamón from a market stall or a specialty shop can access.

Why this specific rule exists

The restriction is about African swine fever and other pork-related animal health concerns in the region, not about the ham itself being unsafe to eat — which is exactly why the commercial-import pathway exists for properly certified, approved producers while personal imports don't qualify.

What this means in practice

  • Don't buy a whole leg or a vacuum-sealed block of jamón planning to check it in your luggage — it's a real risk of confiscation at US customs, not a technicality nobody enforces.
  • Eating it in Spain is obviously fine — the restriction is only about bringing the physical product across the US border.
  • A few specific brands do sell into the US commercially through APHIS-approved processing plants — if you want jamón at home, buying it from a US specialty importer once you're back is the legal path, not carrying it yourself.
  • Other cured meats follow the same logic — chorizo, lomo and similar pork products from the same restricted region carry the same personal-import limitation.

What's actually fine to bring home

Nearly everything else on a typical Spain souvenir list is unrestricted beyond the ordinary rules that apply to any country: ceramics, textiles, leather goods, olive oil, wine (within the standard personal allowance), cheese (most hard, aged cheeses are fine — soft or unpasteurized varieties can be more complicated, so ask if you're unsure), and any non-food craft item travel without special Spain-specific paperwork. Ordinary US personal customs exemptions apply the same way they would for a purchase from any other country — a standard duty-free threshold, then duty above it, nothing unique to Spain.

Shipping instead of carrying

If a Spanish purchase is large, fragile, or simply too good to leave behind despite the ham restriction not applying to it, ask the shop about international shipping rather than defaulting to your suitcase. Many Spanish retailers — especially ones used to a tourist clientele in Barcelona — ship internationally as a normal part of business, and it sidesteps both the breakage risk of checked luggage and any last-minute space crunch in your bags. This is worth asking about even for items that ARE allowed through customs, since a shop shipping directly is often less hassle than hand-carrying something bulky through two or three more flights.

If you're unsure about a specific item

When in doubt about any food product specifically, the safest move is to ask directly at CBP's own resources rather than relying on shop staff or general travel advice, since food-import rules are exactly the kind of regulation that gets enforced strictly and updated periodically. For anything else — ceramics, leather, textiles, art — normal customs declaration and value rules apply, and there's nothing Spain-specific to worry about.

The bottom line

The single thing worth remembering from this whole article: don't plan to bring a leg of jamón home in your suitcase. Everything else on a typical Spain shopping list — ceramics, leather, wine, olive oil, textiles — travels home the same way souvenirs from anywhere else do, under the ordinary personal customs rules every returning traveler already knows.

FAQ

Can I bring jamón ibérico back to the US from Spain?

No — under US federal regulation, cured hams from Spain cannot be brought into the US by travelers in personal luggage. They can only enter as commercial shipments from USDA/FDA-approved Spanish processors.

Will my jamón get confiscated at US customs?

Very likely, if declared or discovered — this is a real, enforced restriction, not a technicality. Don't risk it; enjoy the ham in Spain instead.

Can I buy Spanish ham once I'm back in the US?

Yes — some Spanish producers export commercially through USDA/FDA-approved processing plants, so buying from a US specialty importer once home is the legal way to get it.

Is Spanish wine restricted for US travelers?

No — wine falls under the standard personal customs allowance that applies to alcohol from any country, with duty above the exemption threshold.

What other Spanish food items are restricted for US travelers?

Other cured pork products (chorizo, lomo) from the same restricted European region follow the same personal-import limitation as jamón. Most other food souvenirs — olive oil, hard cheeses, packaged goods — are generally fine.

articles.title: E-Scooters in Barcelona: The Rules and the Fines
articles.excerpt: Barcelona's e-scooter rules are stricter than most American visitors expect — a real helmet law, a €500 sidewalk fine, and mandatory insurance.
articles.content:
Renting an e-scooter feels like the obvious quick fix for getting around Barcelona — until you actually read the rules, which are considerably stricter and more actively enforced than what most American visitors are used to at home. Get them wrong and you're looking at a real fine, not a warning.

Helmets are mandatory, not optional

Since February 1, 2025, Barcelona's municipal ordinance requires a helmet for every rider of an electric scooter — this is a real, currently-enforced rule, not a safety recommendation. If a shared-scooter operator doesn't hand you one, that's on you to sort out before riding, not a loophole that gets you off the hook if you're stopped.

No sidewalks, ever — it's a €500 fine

Riding on sidewalks or any pedestrian area is banned under all circumstances, and it carries one of the steeper fines in the city's mobility rulebook: €500. This is the single most common way tourists get caught out, since sidewalk riding feels intuitive if a bike lane isn't obviously nearby — resist the urge and find the actual lane instead.

Where you actually can ride

  • Bike lanes (over 200 km across the city) — 25 km/h maximum on road-level lanes.
  • Pavement-level cycle paths — 10 km/h maximum, since these run alongside pedestrian areas.
  • Zona-30 streets and shared-priority streets — where cars are already limited to 30 km/h.
  • Designated park routes — 10 km/h maximum.

One rider per scooter, always — no doubling up with a partner or a friend, however short the ride.

Equipment and insurance requirements

Scooters (rented or owned) are required to have front and rear lights, a working brake light, and a horn or bell — a shared-rental scooter should already meet this, but it's worth a glance before you set off. Since July 25, 2025, e-scooter riders in Spain are required to carry insurance under the Automobile Insurance Act; shared/rental operators typically build this into their service, but it's worth confirming rather than assuming, especially with any smaller or less mainstream rental company.

Parking matters too

Scooters can only be left in designated parking zones — locking or leaving one to a random railing, tree, or piece of street furniture isn't just bad etiquette, it's against the ordinance. Shared-rental apps typically show you the nearest valid parking spot directly in the app; use it rather than guessing.

How this compares to home

If you're used to a more relaxed e-scooter culture from a US city, recalibrate before your first ride here. The helmet law alone puts Barcelona ahead of most American cities on enforcement, and the €500 sidewalk fine is a genuinely serious number compared to the token fines (or total non-enforcement) many US visitors are used to. Treat Barcelona's rules as the strict end of what you might have experienced, not the lenient end — assuming home-city norms apply is exactly how visitors end up with a fine they didn't see coming.

Should you even bother with one

Given the rules, the fines, and the fact that Barcelona's metro and walking cover the tourist core extremely well, an e-scooter is really only worth it for a specific point-to-point trip where transit genuinely doesn't work well — not as your default way of getting around. If you do rent one, budget the mental energy to actually follow the rules rather than treating it like a casual toy; the fines are real and the enforcement is active.

What happens if you're stopped

Local police do actively patrol for e-scooter violations, particularly around the tourist-heavy old-city core where sidewalk riding is most tempting and most disruptive to pedestrians. If you're stopped, cooperate and provide ID — a fine issued to a tourist is still a real, collectible fine, not something that quietly disappears once you fly home, so treat it with the same seriousness you would a traffic fine anywhere else.

The bottom line

Barcelona's e-scooter rules are stricter than most visitors expect: a real helmet law, a serious sidewalk fine, speed limits that vary by lane type, and mandatory insurance. None of it is complicated once you know it, but skipping the research before your first ride is exactly how visitors end up with an unplanned €500 souvenir.

FAQ

Do I need a helmet to ride an e-scooter in Barcelona?

Yes — helmets have been mandatory for all e-scooter riders since February 1, 2025, under the city's municipal ordinance.

Can I ride an e-scooter on the sidewalk in Barcelona?

No, under no circumstances — sidewalk riding carries a €500 fine and is one of the most actively enforced rules in the city.

How fast can I go on an e-scooter in Barcelona?

Up to 25 km/h on road-level bike lanes, and 10 km/h on pavement-level cycle paths and designated park routes.

Is insurance required for e-scooters in Barcelona?

Yes — since July 25, 2025, e-scooter riders in Spain must carry insurance under the Automobile Insurance Act. Most shared-rental services build this in, but confirm with smaller operators.

Can two people ride one e-scooter in Barcelona?

No — one rider per scooter is required at all times, regardless of the distance.

articles.title: If You Have an Accident in a Rental Car in Spain
articles.excerpt: The paperwork every rental car carries for exactly this moment, and the calm sequence that gets you through it without making things worse.
articles.content:
A car accident is stressful anywhere, and doing it in a foreign country with a rental car adds a layer of not-knowing-the-process on top. The good news: Spain's procedure is standardized specifically so this isn't guesswork, and most rental cars already carry the one document that matters most.

First: safety, always

Put on hazard lights immediately. Spanish law requires reflective safety vests in the car — put them on before you exit the vehicle, especially on a highway shoulder. Set out the warning triangle if you have one and it's safe to do so. None of the paperwork below matters until everyone is physically safe and visible to oncoming traffic.

The form that makes this simple: the European Accident Statement

Most rental cars carry a European Accident Statement form in the glovebox — known locally as the parte amistoso de accidente or constat amiable. Both drivers fill it out together and sign it: vehicle details, insurance information, a simple diagram of what happened, and each party's account. This is the standard document insurers on both sides expect, and having it properly filled out is what makes your claim straightforward rather than a dispute later.

When to call 112 — and when you don't need to

Call 112 immediately for any injury, significant vehicle damage, or a dispute about who's at fault — Spanish police response for these situations is standard and expected. For a minor, no-injury fender-bender where both parties agree on what happened, many incidents don't require police attendance at all; the accident statement form covers it. Either way, call your rental company's emergency assistance line — it's printed on your rental agreement — before doing anything else with the vehicle itself, since they'll tell you exactly what they need from you.

Document everything before you move anything

  • Photos of both vehicles from multiple angles, and all visible damage specifically.
  • The other party's license, insurance card, and rental agreement (if they're also in a rental) — photograph these documents directly rather than just copying numbers by hand.
  • The surrounding scene — road position, any relevant signage, skid marks if visible — before either vehicle is moved, if it's safe to leave them in place.
  • Never sign anything you don't fully understand — ask for an English copy of any document, or photograph it to translate properly later rather than signing under pressure.

After the immediate moment

Once the scene is documented and everyone's accounted for, contact your travel insurance provider as soon as practical, not just the rental company — a policy with trip-disruption or emergency-assistance coverage may help with anything from a replacement vehicle to a change in your onward plans if the incident affects your itinerary. Keep every piece of paper generated by the incident, including the accident statement, any police reference number if one was issued, and the rental company's own incident report — reimbursement claims move faster with a complete paper trail than a partial one.

Why this connects back to your paperwork before the trip

Everything above assumes you were driving legally in the first place — which for a US visitor means holding the International Driving Permit that's legally required alongside your US license. An insurance claim can be denied on exactly this technicality even when the accident itself wasn't your fault, which is the kind of detail that's easy to overlook until it costs you. Confirming your rental's insurance coverage and excess terms before you ever get behind the wheel is the preparation that actually pays off in a moment like this.

The bottom line

Safety first, the accident statement form second, 112 only when the situation actually calls for it, and thorough documentation before anything gets moved. Spain's process is designed to be straightforward specifically so a stressful moment doesn't have to be a confusing one — the paperwork already exists in your glovebox for exactly this purpose.

FAQ

Do I need to call the police after a car accident in Spain?

Only for injury, significant damage, or a dispute about fault — call 112. For a minor, no-injury incident with agreement on what happened, the European Accident Statement form usually covers it without police attendance.

What is the European Accident Statement?

A standard form (parte amistoso de accidente) most rental cars carry in the glovebox, filled out and signed by both drivers, documenting the incident for both insurers.

Do I have to wear a safety vest if I have an accident in Spain?

Yes — Spanish law requires reflective safety vests in the car, and you should put one on before exiting the vehicle, especially on a highway.

Who should I call first after a rental car accident in Spain?

Ensure everyone's safety first, then call your rental company's emergency assistance line (on your rental agreement) and 112 if there's injury, major damage, or a fault dispute.

Can my insurance claim be denied after an accident in Spain?

Yes, on technicalities — most notably driving without the legally required International Driving Permit, even if the accident wasn't your fault. Confirm your paperwork before you drive.

articles.title: The Activities That Void Your Policy in Spain
articles.excerpt: Travel insurance rarely covers everything you'd assume — the specific gaps that catch travelers doing perfectly normal Barcelona activities.
articles.content:
Travel insurance feels like a blanket safety net until you actually read the exclusions page — and a handful of the activities it excludes are things a normal Barcelona trip genuinely involves, not exotic extreme sports. Knowing the gaps before you need them is the whole point of reading this now instead of after an incident.

Driving without the right paperwork

This is the one that catches Americans most often: driving a rental car in Spain without the International Driving Permit that's legally required alongside your US license. If you're in an accident and it comes out that you were driving without the IDP, a claim can be denied on that technicality — even when the accident itself genuinely wasn't your fault. The fix is cheap and takes ten minutes at a AAA office before you fly; there's no good reason to skip it.

Riding without the right license class

Mopeds, motorcycles and certain scooters require a specific license class under Spanish law, and riding one without it isn't just a legal problem — it typically voids the relevant portion of a travel insurance policy too. This matters more than it sounds like it should for a city trip: rental mopeds are a common, casual-feeling activity for a Costa Brava day trip, and travelers don't always think to check the license requirement before hopping on.

E-scooters without the now-mandatory insurance

Spain's Automobile Insurance Act now requires e-scooter riders to carry insurance (in force since July 2025) — riding without it isn't just a legal gap, it can be a violation of your OWN travel policy's terms too, layering one problem on top of another if something goes wrong. Most shared-rental scooter services build the required coverage in, but it's worth confirming rather than assuming, especially with smaller operators.

The genuinely "extreme" exclusions

Beyond the driving-related gaps above, standard policies typically name specific high-risk activities they exclude outright — think cliff-diving, certain technical watersports, or off-piste-equivalent adventure activities. These are usually listed explicitly in a policy's exclusions section rather than left to interpretation, so the fix here is simple: actually read that section of your specific policy rather than assuming standard coverage extends to anything adventurous you might do.

Read the policy, not the marketing page

Every travel insurance provider's marketing copy emphasizes what's covered; the exclusions live in a separate, less-promoted section of the actual policy document — that's where the specifics above actually get spelled out, in the provider's own exact wording rather than a generic summary like this one. Before this trip specifically, it's worth the ten minutes to search that document for "exclusions," "licensing," and "permitted drivers" rather than assuming your policy works the way a previous one did, since terms vary meaningfully between providers even for ostensibly similar coverage.

Why this is worth ten minutes before you fly

Every exclusion on this list has the same fix: check it before you need it, not after. The IDP costs about $20 and ten minutes at AAA. Confirming a moped rental's license requirement is one question to the rental shop. Checking whether your e-scooter rental includes required insurance is one line in the app's terms. None of this is complicated — it's just the kind of preparation that's invisible right up until the moment it matters enormously.

The bottom line

Travel insurance exclusions in Spain cluster around a specific theme: driving or riding something without the legally required credential for it. Get the IDP before you fly, confirm license requirements before renting a moped, confirm insurance coverage before an e-scooter ride, and actually read your specific policy's named exclusions for anything more adventurous. That's the whole list, and it's entirely avoidable with a small amount of preparation.

FAQ

Does travel insurance cover me if I drive without an International Driving Permit in Spain?

Often not fully — a claim can be denied on this technicality even if an accident wasn't your fault, since the IDP is legally required for US drivers in Spain.

Do I need a special license to rent a moped in Spain?

Yes, depending on the vehicle's engine size — riding without the correct license class can void the relevant part of your travel insurance in addition to being illegal.

Is riding an e-scooter covered by travel insurance in Spain?

It depends on whether the required insurance under Spain's Automobile Insurance Act is in place — most shared-rental services include it, but confirm with smaller operators rather than assuming.

What activities does travel insurance typically exclude in Spain?

Beyond driving/riding without proper licensing, standard policies often name specific high-risk activities (cliff-diving, certain watersports) explicitly in their exclusions — always check your specific policy's list.

How do I avoid voiding my travel insurance in Spain?

Get the International Driving Permit before you fly, confirm license requirements before renting any motorized two-wheeler, confirm e-scooter insurance coverage, and read your policy's named exclusions.

articles.title: Renting a Car in Spain: What the Law Says, What the Desk Says
articles.excerpt: Spanish law sets the real rules; the rental desk has its own separate playbook of upsells and holds — knowing which is which saves both money and hassle.
articles.content:
Two separate rulebooks govern a Spanish car rental: what the law actually requires, and what the rental desk will try to get you to agree to. They overlap in places, but conflating them costs travelers money and, occasionally, a legitimate insurance claim. Here's each one, kept clearly apart.

What the law actually says

Spain drives on the right. US drivers need their US license plus an International Driving Permit (IDP) — this one is a real legal requirement, not upsell material, and it's worth getting from AAA before you fly (about $20, ten minutes). The blood-alcohol limit is 0.05% (0.03% for novice drivers) — stricter than most US states. None of this is negotiable or desk-dependent; it's Spanish traffic law regardless of which company you rent from.

What the desk actually does

This is where a second, separate set of practices kicks in — none of it illegal, all of it worth knowing before you're standing at the counter tired from a flight.

The deposit hold

Expect a hold (not a charge) on a credit card sized to the vehicle's damage excess — this is standard, and a debit card is often refused outright for this purpose, so bring an actual credit card with enough headroom.

The insurance upsell

Desk staff routinely offer their own collision-damage-waiver product at a real markup over what a third-party excess-insurance policy — bought online before your trip — costs for equivalent coverage. Buying third-party cover in advance is usually the better value if you're comfortable filing a reimbursement claim after the fact rather than avoiding the excess hold entirely at the counter.

Fuel policy

Almost always full-to-full — you receive it full, you return it full, or you pay a penalty rate on whatever's missing. This is the fairest option when you're given a choice, so take it over prepaid-fuel alternatives.

Cross-border restrictions

If a France or Andorra day trip is even a possibility, ask explicitly — some Spain-based rentals restrict or surcharge crossing the border, and this is exactly the kind of detail that isn't obvious from the booking confirmation alone.

Where the two rulebooks actually intersect

The one place law and desk practice genuinely collide: if you skip the IDP (a legal requirement) and something goes wrong, it's not just a traffic-law problem — it can also void the insurance coverage the desk sold you, since most policies (theirs and any third-party one) assume you were driving legally in the first place. The legal requirement and the insurance product aren't separate concerns; the first is a precondition for the second actually paying out.

What to check before you leave the counter

Before driving away, walk around the car with a staff member and note every existing scratch, dent or wheel scuff on the paperwork — photograph each one with a timestamp, not just a mental note. This protects you from being charged for pre-existing damage at return, which is a far more common dispute than anything related to an actual accident. It costs five extra minutes at pickup and it's the single best protection against a surprise charge on your card after you've already flown home.

Should you even rent a car for Barcelona

For the city itself, no — the low-emission zone (ZBE), scarce and expensive parking, and break-in risk make a car a genuine liability rather than a convenience. The right move is renting only for a specific day trip (Costa Brava is the classic case), picking the car up the morning you need it and dropping it off the same day or on departure, rather than holding a rental for your entire Barcelona stay.

The bottom line

The law's requirements (IDP, BAC limit, driving side) are fixed and identical everywhere. The desk's practices (deposit holds, insurance upsells, fuel policy, cross-border rules) vary by company and are worth navigating deliberately rather than accepting on autopilot. Handle both — legal paperwork before you fly, desk-practice awareness at the counter — and a Costa Brava day-trip rental is a smooth, uneventful part of the itinerary rather than a source of surprise costs.

FAQ

Do I legally need an International Driving Permit to rent a car in Spain?

Yes — it's legally required alongside your US license for driving in Spain, not just a rental-company preference. Get it from AAA before you fly.

Can I use a debit card for a car rental deposit in Spain?

Often not — many rental companies refuse debit cards for the deposit hold and require an actual credit card with enough available credit.

Should I buy the rental company's insurance or my own?

Third-party excess insurance bought before your trip is usually cheaper than the desk's own collision-damage-waiver product, if you're comfortable with a reimbursement-style claim process.

What fuel policy do Spanish car rentals use?

Almost always full-to-full — you receive and return the car with a full tank, or pay a penalty rate for any shortfall. Take this option over prepaid fuel if given a choice.

Should I rent a car for my whole Barcelona trip?

No — rent only for a specific day trip like the Costa Brava. Barcelona itself has a low-emission zone, expensive scarce parking, and real break-in risk that make a car a liability in the city.
